title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The object of a verb changes shape. aqua is 'water' as the subject and aquam as the thing wanted — Aquam volō. English marks this on nobody except a handful of pronouns (I/me, he/him), so the habit of leaving a noun alone has to be unlearned on every noun.

'I do not want' is one word, and it is not nōn volō. Latin builds nōlō out of the same verb with the negative fused in — nōlō aquam. nōn volō exists and means the same, but nōlō is what a Roman reaches for, and it is a separate verb to learn rather than a phrase to assemble.

An infinitive comes BEFORE the verb that governs it: Aquam bibere volō, 'water to-drink I-want'. English puts 'want' first and the infinitive after it, so the whole sentence arrives in reverse order — and the object goes first of all, because it belongs to bibere.

habeō does exactly what English 'have' does: Librum habeō. It is the one construction in this module with nothing to unlearn — which is worth noticing, because M1's name sentence used a 'to me' instead and this is not that.

Needing is impersonal and takes a strange case: Mihi opus est aquā — 'for me there is need with water'. Nobody is the subject except the need itself, and the thing needed goes into the ablative, which is neither the subject's shape nor the object's. It is the first case in the course that is neither.

The ablative of a first-declension noun is the nominative with a long vowel and nothing else: aqua becomes aquā. That bar is the whole ending. Drop it in writing and you have written the subject; drop it in speech and a Roman hears the subject.

nōn sits directly in front of what it negates and there is no helper to build: Nōn habeō librum. English needs a 'do' that carries the negative and means nothing; Latin has no such word, so there is nothing here that corresponds to 'don't'.

pānis is bread, not a pan; and while English 'aquatic' keeps aqua, English 'volition' keeps volō and English 'habit' keeps habeō — none of which helps you guess which shape to write. The cognates tell you the meaning and lie about the grammar.

words.note: 'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā after opus est. Three shapes of one word, and the -m is what marks it as the thing being wanted.
'I want' — irregular, and the only verb for wanting: volō 'I want', vult 'he/she wants'. It takes an object or an infinitive, and both come before it.

sentences.trap: aqua became aquam. English leaves 'water' alone whether it is doing the wanting or being wanted, so nothing warns you that the noun has to move.
sentences.sound: A-quam VO-lō. The qu is the k-plus-w of 'quick'. The ō of volō is long and it is what says 'I'.

mistake.why: The noun left in its subject shape. Written like this the sentence says 'water, I want' with two subjects and no object — and it is the single commonest error an English speaker makes in Latin, because English nouns never move.

sentences.usage: Said at a table, or to anyone who can fetch it.

words.note: 'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā after opus est. Here it belongs to bibere, not to volō.
'To drink', the infinitive — the shape a dictionary lists second. bibō 'I drink', bibis 'you drink', bibit 'he/she drinks'. The -re ending is what makes it 'to'.
'I want' — irregular, and the only verb for wanting: volō 'I want', vult 'he/she wants'. It takes an object or an infinitive, and both come before it.

sentences.sound: A-quam BI-be-re VO-lō. Three words, three stresses on first syllables. Say the -re of bibere lightly; it carries no weight.

'I have', and it does exactly what English 'have' does: habeō 'I have', habēs 'you have', habet 'he/she has'. Nothing here needs unlearning.

sentences.trap: This is not how M1 said your name. Mihi nōmen est used a 'to me' because that is the idiom for a name; for an ordinary possession Latin has habeō and uses it.
sentences.sound: LI-brum ha-BE-ō. Say the h. habeō is three syllables — ha-BE-o — with the stress on the middle one.

sentences.usage: Said about anything you are carrying or own.

words.note: 'I' has more than one shape: ego does the acting, mihi is 'to me / for me'. Needing, like liking, puts you in this one rather than in the subject's chair.
'Need' — a noun, and the subject of this sentence. It never changes shape here, because opus est is a fixed pairing: 'there is need'.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā as the thing needed. The bar over the a is the whole of that third ending.

sentences.trap: You are not the subject and the water is not the object. The need is the subject, you are the one it exists for, and the water is in a third case that does neither job — so nothing in the English sentence maps onto anything in the Latin one.
sentences.sound: MI-hi O-pus est a-QUA. The last word is the one to get right: a long ā at the end, held, and the stress pulled onto it.

variations.changed: a different thing needed, in the same third case

mistake.why: The thing needed put in the object shape, because 'I need water' looks like it has an object. opus est is not a verb that takes objects — it is a noun and 'to be', and what it pairs with goes into the ablative: aquā.

sentences.usage: Said when you need something rather than merely want it.
sentences.mnemonic: 'For me there is need' — and the thing is what the need is WITH.

words.note: 'Bread': pānis as the subject, pānem as the object, pāne as the thing needed. It is not a pan — the English word that kept it is 'pantry', the bread room.
'I want' — irregular, and the only verb for wanting: volō 'I want', vult 'he/she wants'. It takes an object or an infinitive, and both come before it.

sentences.trap: pānis does not become pānam. Its object shape is pānem, because it belongs to a different family of nouns from aqua — the ending you need depends on the word, not on the job.
sentences.sound: PA-nem VO-lō. The ā is long and stressed; the -em is light and quick.

words.note: 'Not', and it goes straight in front of the verb. Nothing corresponds to English 'do not': there is no helper to hang the negative on, so nōn sits on the verb itself.
'I have', and it does exactly what English 'have' does: habeō 'I have', habēs 'you have', habet 'he/she has'. Nothing here needs unlearning.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one. The e drops out as soon as an ending is added.

sentences.trap: There is no 'do' in it. English cannot negate a verb without borrowing a helper; Latin puts nōn in front and the sentence is finished.
sentences.sound: NON ha-BE-ō LI-brum. Hold the ō of nōn — it is long, and the word is doing all the negating on its own.

words.note: 'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā after opus est. Here it belongs to bibere, not to nōlō.
